quizTitle: Project Management - Module 7: Project Quality Management

questions.text: The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) answers the question "What features must we build?" Which question does Project Quality Management answer?
options: Who will build each feature?
When will each feature be delivered?
How well must those features perform?
How much will each feature cost?
questions.explanation: The RTM maps stakeholder needs to functional code ("What features must we build?"). Quality Management evaluates stability, reliability and stress limits under load ("How well must those features perform?").

questions.text: Match each measure to the area it belongs to: requirements traceability (the RTM) or project quality management.

pairs.term: Maps stakeholder needs directly to functional code components
Evaluates stability, reliability, and stress limits under load

questions.explanation: The RTM is about feature mapping, measured by completeness (100% functional coverage). Quality management is about performance standards, measured by user satisfaction (zero systemic outages).

questions.text: A system that delivers 100% of the features in its RTM but crashes under peak load still counts as a quality success, because every requirement was built.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Meeting 100% of RTM features while crashing under peak load is a critical quality failure.

questions.text: How is quality defined?
options: The degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfills explicit and implicit requirements reliably
A technical rank given to deliverables with the same use but different feature complexity
The number of features a deliverable offers
How modern and polished the user interface looks
questions.explanation: Quality is the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfills explicit and implicit requirements reliably. Its keyword is conformance. A technical rank by feature complexity is grade.

questions.text: How is grade defined?
options: The number of defects found per million opportunities
The degree to which a deliverable fulfills its requirements reliably
The score a deliverable gets in User Acceptance Testing
A category or technical rank given to deliverables sharing the same functional use but varying feature complexity
questions.explanation: Grade is a category or technical rank for deliverables with the same functional use but varying feature complexity. Its keyword is complexity, while quality's is conformance.

questions.text: Match each term to its keyword.
questions.explanation: Quality = conformance (does it fulfill its requirements reliably?). Grade = complexity (how feature-rich is it, among deliverables with the same use?).

questions.text: A basic open-source text editor and a fully featured enterprise IDE with AI assistants are both used to edit code. What is the difference between them?
options: Quality: the IDE is high quality and the editor is low quality
Grade: they share the same functional use but differ in feature complexity
Conformance: only the IDE fulfills its requirements
Nothing: they are the same grade and the same quality
questions.explanation: They differ in grade: same functional use, different feature complexity. That says nothing about quality; a basic editor that never crashes can be high quality.

questions.text: A lightweight command-line utility has very few features, but it always runs without crashing. How would you describe it?
options: Low quality, because it has few features
High grade and low quality
Unacceptable, because low grade is never allowed
High quality: it reliably does what it is required to do
questions.explanation: Executing without crashes means it conforms to its requirements, so it has high quality. Few features is a matter of grade, and low grade is acceptable if planned.

questions.text: Low quality is acceptable if it was planned, just like low grade.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The Golden Rule: low grade is acceptable if planned. Low quality is never acceptable.

questions.text: Which description fits Quality Assurance (QA)?
options: Process-oriented, focused on defect prevention
Product-oriented, focused on defect detection
Finance-oriented, focused on the cost of each defect
Customer-oriented, focused on post-launch reviews
questions.explanation: QA is process-oriented and focused on defect prevention: coding standards, CI/CD pipelines, architecture guidelines.

questions.text: Which description fits Quality Control (QC)?
options: Process-oriented, focused on defect prevention
Schedule-oriented, focused on finishing testing on time
Product-oriented, focused on defect detection
Planning-oriented, focused on writing the quality policy
questions.explanation: QC is product-oriented and focused on defect detection: execution testing, security and load audits, UAT sign-offs.

questions.text: Classify each activity as Quality Assurance (QA) or Quality Control (QC).

pairs.term: Automating deployment and review gates (CI/CD pipelines)
Running automated unit and integration tests

questions.explanation: QA shapes the process so defects are prevented (coding standards, CI/CD pipelines, architecture guidelines). QC inspects the product so defects are detected (execution testing, security and load audits, user acceptance).

questions.text: Which statement correctly contrasts QA and QC?
options: QA detects defects in the finished product; QC prevents defects in the process
QA prevents defects through the process; QC detects defects in the product
QA and QC are two names for the same testing phase
QA is done only by the client; QC is done only by developers
questions.explanation: QA is process-oriented prevention; QC is product-oriented detection.

questions.text: Classify each cost into its Cost of Quality (CoQ) category.

pairs.term: SLA penalties, lost sales and lawsuits

questions.explanation: Prevention: stop defects being made (code reviews, training, test scripts). Appraisal: check for defects (audits, scans, pen and load tests). Internal failure: defects fixed before release (rework, re-testing). External failure: defects that reach production (downtime, SLA penalties, lost sales, lawsuits).

questions.text: In the Cost of Quality framework, the Cost of Conformance (money spent to avoid failure) is made up of which two categories?
options: Prevention costs and appraisal costs
Internal failure costs and external failure costs
Prevention costs and external failure costs
Appraisal costs and internal failure costs
questions.explanation: Cost of Conformance = 1. Prevention + 2. Appraisal. Cost of Non-Conformance = 3. Internal Failure + 4. External Failure.

questions.text: In the Cost of Quality framework, the Cost of Non-Conformance (money spent because of failure) is made up of which two categories?
options: Prevention costs and appraisal costs
Appraisal costs and external failure costs
Prevention costs and internal failure costs
Internal failure costs and external failure costs
questions.explanation: Cost of Non-Conformance = Internal Failure (caught before release) + External Failure (reached production).

questions.text: A defect is found during testing, and the team spends three days on emergency fixes and re-testing before the release goes out. Which Cost of Quality category do these costs fall under?
options: Prevention cost
Appraisal cost
Internal failure cost
External failure cost
questions.explanation: The defect was handled before release, so rework, emergency fixes and re-testing overhead are internal failure costs.

questions.text: A week after launch, a production outage leads to SLA penalties, lost sales, and a lawsuit. Which Cost of Quality category are these?
options: Prevention cost
Appraisal cost
Internal failure cost
External failure cost
questions.explanation: The failure reached production, so downtime, SLA penalties, lost sales and lawsuits are external failure costs.

questions.text: Investing in prevention (QA) always costs less than paying for external failures.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. It's one of the module's core takeaways: investing in Prevention (QA) always costs less than External Failures.

questions.text: Match each of the 7 basic quality tools to the purpose it serves in IT.
questions.explanation: Root cause analysis: Fishbone. Priority & tallying (bug prioritization): Pareto, Histogram, Check Sheet. Process control (operational stability): Scatter, Flowchart, Run Chart, Control Chart.

questions.text: A team needs to find the root cause of an API latency problem by sorting possible causes into categories such as People, Infrastructure, Code Architecture, and Dependencies. Which quality tool fits best?
options: Pareto chart
Run chart
Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram
Check sheet
questions.explanation: A Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram categorizes causes by origin (e.g., People, Infrastructure, Code Architecture, Dependencies) to locate the root cause.

questions.text: Applied to system downtime, what does the Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule) say?
options: 20% of system downtime originates from 80% of critical defects
80% of system downtime originates from 20% of critical defects
80% of defects are found by 20% of the testers
Systems should be up at least 80% of the time
questions.explanation: A Pareto chart shows that 80% of system downtime comes from 20% of critical defects (e.g., unindexed queries and memory leaks), so fixing those few removes most of the downtime.

questions.text: A fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram ranks defects from most to least frequent to show the 80/20 split.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Ranking defects for the 80/20 split is the Pareto chart. A fishbone diagram categorizes possible causes by origin to find a root cause.

questions.text: On a control chart with process mean μ and standard deviation σ, where are the Upper Control Limit (UCL) and Lower Control Limit (LCL) set?
options: UCL = μ + 1σ, LCL = μ − 1σ
UCL = μ + 2σ, LCL = μ − 2σ
UCL = μ + 3σ, LCL = μ − 3σ
UCL = μ + 6σ, LCL = μ − 6σ
questions.explanation: Control charts use ±3σ boundaries: UCL = +3σ, LCL = −3σ, with the process mean μ as the baseline.

questions.text: A control chart tracks API response time across build iterations. The mean is 200 ms, the UCL is 260 ms, and the LCL is 140 ms. The last seven builds measured 210, 215, 208, 220, 212, 225, and 218 ms. What should the team conclude?
options: The process is in control, because every point is inside the control limits
Nothing, because the values are still close to the mean
The process is out of control, because a point is above the UCL
The process is out of control and needs investigation, because 7 consecutive points are above the mean
questions.explanation: By the Seven Run Rule, 7 consecutive points on one side of the mean mean the process is out of control, even though all are inside the limits (none is above 260 ms). It points to systemic bias.

questions.text: As long as every data point on a control chart stays between the UCL and the LCL, the process is in control.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Under the Seven Run Rule, 7 consecutive points on one side of the mean make the process out of control, even inside the limits.

questions.text: API response times on a control chart show seven builds in a row above the mean, all inside the control limits. What kind of problem does this typically signal?
options: Non-random variation, such as memory degradation or background process strain
Random noise that can be safely ignored
A one-off spike caused by a single bad request
That the control limits were set too wide and should be removed
questions.explanation: The Seven Run Rule flags non-random variation (systemic bias), such as memory degradation or background process strain, which needs immediate investigation.

questions.text: Six Sigma's operational target is no more than ___ Defects Per Million Opportunities (DPMO). (Enter the number.)
questions.explanation: Six Sigma targets ≤ 3.4 DPMO.

questions.text: Put the 5 phases of DMAIC, the Six Sigma framework, in order.
questions.explanation: DMAIC = Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control.

questions.text: Match each DMAIC phase to what it involves in an IT project.
questions.explanation: Define the CTQ (Critical to Quality) specs, Measure the baseline, Analyze to isolate process flaws, Improve by refactoring and automating, and Control to prevent regression.

questions.text: Read the case above. Which option does the quality gate trade-off strategy recommend?
questions.context:
FinTech Express has 50 open defects before launch, and a $500k marketing campaign is tied to the launch date.

SeverityCountExample
1: Critical3 (6%)Intermittent payment transaction crashes under peak load
2: Moderate7 (14%)Timeout during PDF statement generation
3: Minor40 (80%)Misaligned button padding and help page typos
options: Full Delay: delay the launch 2 weeks to fix all 50 defects
Launch As-Is: override the QA gate and deploy on schedule
Targeted Gate: hotfix the Sev-1 and Sev-2 bugs and defer the cosmetic issues
Cancel the launch and the marketing campaign
questions.explanation: The Targeted Gate is recommended: it protects transaction revenue while meeting the campaign deadline. A full delay wastes the $500k marketing spend and loses momentum; launching as-is risks critical transaction failures and severe brand damage.

questions.text: Read the case above. Under the Targeted Gate option, how many defects get hotfixed before launch?
questions.context:
A payment app has 50 open defects before launch, with a $500k marketing campaign tied to the launch date.

SeverityCountExample
1: Critical3Intermittent payment transaction crashes under peak load
2: Moderate7Timeout during PDF statement generation
3: Minor40Misaligned button padding and help page typos

The Targeted Gate hotfixes every Severity 1 and Severity 2 defect and defers the cosmetic ones.
questions.explanation: Sev-1 + Sev-2 = 3 + 7 = 10 hotfixed. The 40 minor (cosmetic) defects are deferred.

questions.text: Read the case above. Which quality tool would best justify the Targeted Gate in a meeting with the Lead Architect and the CMO?
questions.context: Before launch, a QC audit logs 50 open defects: 3 critical (payment crashes under peak load), 7 moderate (PDF statement timeouts) and 40 minor (button padding, help page typos). The PM proposes hotfixing the 10 critical and moderate defects and deferring the 40 minor ones, so a $500k marketing campaign can launch on time.
options: Scatter diagram
Pareto chart
Control chart
Flowchart
questions.explanation: The decision rests on the 80/20 split: 20% of defects (Sev-1 and Sev-2) carry the real risk, 80% are cosmetic. A Pareto chart shows that split at a glance.

questions.text: A launch has 50 open defects (10 critical or moderate, 40 cosmetic) and a $500k marketing campaign tied to the launch date. Match each option to its main downside or upside.
allChoices: Wasted $500k marketing spend and lost market momentum
Critical transaction failures and severe brand damage
Protects transaction revenue while meeting the campaign deadline

pairs.term: Full Delay (fix all 50, launch 2 weeks late)
pairs.match: Wasted $500k marketing spend and lost market momentum
Critical transaction failures and severe brand damage
Protects transaction revenue while meeting the campaign deadline

questions.explanation: Full Delay costs the campaign; Launch As-Is risks critical failures and brand damage; the Targeted Gate gets the best of both, which is why it's recommended.

questions.text: A team launches on time after hotfixing all critical and moderate defects, deferring 40 cosmetic ones. What is the proper way to handle the deferred defects?
options: Structure a formal Change Request for them, without degrading the approved scope
Fix them quietly in production whenever someone has spare time
Delete them from the defect log, since they're only cosmetic
Add them to the Project Charter as exclusions
questions.explanation: Deferred defects go through a formal Change Request, structured so the approved scope isn't degraded. Deleting or quietly fixing them bypasses change management.

questions.text: Which of these are core takeaways of Project Quality Management? (Select all that apply.)
options: Quality is non-negotiable; grade is planned complexity
Investing in prevention (QA) always costs less than external failures
Targeted gates balance launch deadlines with technical risk using DMAIC metrics
A product with more features is always higher quality
QC alone is enough, so QA can be skipped to save time
questions.explanation: The three takeaways: quality is non-negotiable while grade is planned complexity; prevention (QA) costs less than external failures; targeted gates balance deadlines with technical risk using DMAIC metrics.
